50.title: A wife at the well (Genesis 24:1–27)
50.hook: the servant's test: the one who offers water to him and to his camels too
50.howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness such as visiting the sick, comforting mourners and helping a bride and groom, among the pillars of Jewish life, and communities often organize them through volunteer groups.

segments.voice: Last week ended with Sarah's burial, and a grave bought at full price. Your line was grief deserves ground. Whose memory did you honor? A new week, and day fifty.

Abraham is old now, and Isaac needs a wife. So Abraham sends his senior servant, the elder of his house, on a long journey back to the family's homeland, with ten camels loaded with gifts. The servant arrives outside a town at evening, the hour when the young women come out to draw water. He makes the camels kneel by the well. And he's stuck. How do you pick a person for someone else's whole life? So he prays, in the old JPS translation: "O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, send me, I pray Thee, good speed this day, and show kindness unto my master Abraham." Abraham has told him where to look: among the family. But which young woman? So he sets a test. Not looks. Not money. Something much smaller, and much harder to fake.
screen: `TEN CAMELS AND A LONG ROAD.` → `EVENING AT THE WELL.` → `HOW DO YOU CHOOSE?`

segments.voice: Here's the test. I'll ask a girl for a drink. If she says, drink, and I'll water your camels too, she's the one. And before he's even finished praying, Rebekah comes out with a jar on her shoulder. She fills it. He runs up and asks for a sip. She says, drink, my lord, and hurries to lower the jar. And then, without being asked: "I will draw for thy camels also, until they have done drinking." Stop and see it. Ten camels, after a long road, and every one of them thirsty. That's trip after trip down to the spring, jar after jar, for a stranger's animals, in the evening. The Torah says she ran. That's chesed. It's a big word in the Hebrew Bible, and it's hard to translate. Kindness. Loving-kindness. Loyal love. Mercy. At its heart, chesed is kindness that goes past what's owed: past fair, past asked. The servant's prayer uses it, show chesed to my master. And when he realizes she's the one, he bows and blesses God, who has not forsaken His mercy, chesed again. The prophet Micah later sums up what God asks of a person: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly. That mercy is chesed. And the Mishnah says the whole world stands on three things: Torah, worship, and acts of loving-kindness. The servant wasn't looking for someone who'd do what was asked. He was looking for someone who'd notice the camels.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think about the requests people make of you in a normal day: pass the salt, send me that file, can you pick up milk. Now think about the camels behind the request. The thing nobody asked for but would make their day lighter. The coworker who asked for the file but is clearly drowning. The parent who asked about dinner but is lonely. Pick one person. Picture the extra thing. If you pray, you can ask to notice. The bell holds the time.
Chesed. Loving-kindness: kindness that goes past what's owed. Rebekah watering ten camels for a stranger.
Your line: water the camels too. Today, offer one kind of help nobody asked you for. Day fifty.

51.title: Rebekah says "I will go" (Genesis 24:57–58)
51.hook: her family asks her, and she chooses for herself
51.howItsDone: At Jewish weddings that keep the bedeken, the veiling of the bride, the blessing Rebekah's family gave her is said over the bride; Jewish law requires the bride's own consent to the marriage.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chesed, kindness past what's owed, and ten thirsty camels. Your line was water the camels too. What help did you offer unasked? Day fifty-one.

Rebekah runs home and tells her family about the stranger at the well. Her brother Laban comes out, sees the gold bracelets, and invites the servant in. Food is set out, and the servant says: I won't eat until I've told you why I'm here. And he tells the whole story again, every detail, the prayer, the camels, the water. The rabbis noticed how long the Torah lets him talk, and said: even the everyday speech of the patriarchs' servants is precious. The family agrees to the match. But in the morning, when the servant wants to leave right away, her mother and brother hesitate. Let her stay with us a while, ten days at least. The servant says, don't hold me back. And then the family does something the rabbis would later build a law on.
screen: `THE WHOLE STORY, TOLD AGAIN.` → `STAY TEN DAYS.` → `DON'T HOLD ME BACK.`

segments.voice: In the old JPS translation, they say: "We will call the damsel, and inquire at her mouth." They ask her. And they put it to her directly: "Wilt thou go with this man?" And she answers in one Hebrew word, elech: "I will go." Two things to notice. First, the asking. Rashi, the medieval commentator, reads this verse as a law: from here we learn that a woman may not be married off without her consent. And Jewish law, as it developed, holds that a grown woman's marriage needs her own yes. The Torah could have skipped her answer. Instead it pauses to show someone asking her first. Second, the answer. Some commentators notice that Rebekah's yes sounds like Abraham's call: she, too, leaves her land, her birthplace and her father's house, for a man and a place she's never seen. She goes before she knows, just as he did. Her family sends her off with a blessing: our sister, may you become thousands upon thousands. At the bedeken, a Jewish wedding custom, those words are said to the bride as her veil is lowered. And at the end of the chapter, she arrives. Isaac has gone out to the field at evening, the Torah says, to meditate. She sees him from her camel and veils herself. He brings her into his mother Sarah's tent, and he loves her, and he is comforted after his mother's death. The Torah says it plainly: he loved her. And it started with a question: will you go?

Then picture yourself answering the way Rebekah did, with one short word. I'll go. How does that feel in your chest? If you pray, you can ask for a clear yes. The bell holds the time.

52.title: Isaac redigs the wells (Genesis 26:17–22)
52.hook: the quiet patriarch reopens his father's wells and gives them their old names
52.howItsDone: Jewish tradition sets three daily prayers, and one teaching links the afternoon prayer, Minchah, to Isaac; the story of the wells is read in the Torah portion Toldot.

segments.voice: Yesterday: elech, one word, her own choice. Your line was ask her first. Did you ask before deciding, or say yes to something good? Day fifty-two.

Of the three fathers of Genesis, Isaac is the quiet one. Abraham gets the journeys and the arguments. Jacob gets the ladder and the wrestling. Isaac gets a few chapters, and in the middle of them, a story about wells. Abraham has died. There's a famine, and Isaac settles among the Philistines, in a place called Gerar. He plants, and the land gives back a hundredfold. He grows rich, and the neighbors grow jealous. Years before, Abraham's servants had dug wells there. Now the Philistines have stopped them all up, filled them with dirt. In a dry land, a well is life. Blocking one is a way of saying: you don't belong here. Today: what the quiet son does with his father's buried wells.
screen: `THE QUIET PATRIARCH.` → `A HUNDREDFOLD, AND JEALOUSY.` → `THE WELLS FILLED WITH DIRT.`

segments.voice: Isaac doesn't fight. He moves, and he digs. He opens up his father's old wells again, one by one. And then a lovely detail, in the old JPS translation: "and he called their names after the names by which his father had called them." He doesn't rename them after himself. He gives them back their old names. Then his servants dig new wells. At the first one, local herdsmen argue: the water is ours. Isaac names it Esek, quarrel, and moves on. At the second, they argue again. He names it Sitnah, enmity, and moves on. At the third, nobody fights. He names it Rehoboth, which means wide spaces, room: "For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land." Some Jewish teachers read this as a picture of every generation. The wells our parents dug, the practices, the prayers, the Shabbat table, get stopped up over time, filled with dirt, forgotten. Each generation has to dig them out again, and it often honors them by keeping their old names. Only then do new wells come. And Isaac adds his own. One view in the Talmud says that each of the fathers began one of the three daily prayers: Abraham the morning prayer, Jacob the evening, and Isaac the afternoon. For Isaac, it points to the day he went out to the field at evening to meditate, the day Rebekah first saw him. In that view, the quiet one gave Jews the prayer in the middle of the busy day. He didn't build anything new and grand. He kept digging until the water came.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of a good habit you used to have and let go: a morning walk, a phone call with your grandmother, reading before bed, lighting candles on Friday, a few minutes of quiet. Something that once gave you water. Picture it filled in with dirt, not by anyone's fault, just by life. Now picture digging it out, one shovelful. What would the first small step be? If you pray, you can ask for the strength to go back. The bell holds the time.
Rehoboth, Hebrew for wide spaces, room, the well where no one argued. The quiet patriarch opens his father's stopped-up wells and gives them back their old names.
Your line: redig the well. Today, go back to one good old habit, just once, and see if the water's still there. Day fifty-two.

53.title: A bowl of red stew (Genesis 25:19–34)
53.hook: twins who wrestle in the womb, and a birthright sold for lentils
53.howItsDone: Jews read the birth of Jacob and Esau in the Torah portion Toldot; mourners are often served round foods such as lentils or eggs at the first meal after a funeral, a custom linked to this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rehoboth, the well with no quarrel, and the old names given back. Your line was redig the well. Which old habit did you dig out? Day fifty-three.

The Torah steps back, to how Isaac's family began. Rebekah can't have children, and Isaac prays for her, and she conceives. Twins. And they fight before they're born. The pregnancy is so hard she asks God what's happening, and the answer is startling. In the old JPS translation: "Two nations are in thy womb." Two peoples, and the elder shall serve the younger. The first comes out red and hairy all over, and they call him Esau. The second comes out holding his brother's heel, and they call him Jacob, Yaakov, from akev, heel. Esau grows up a hunter, a man of the fields. Jacob, the Torah says, is "a quiet man, dwelling in tents." Isaac loves Esau. Rebekah loves Jacob. Any family with a favorite can hear where this is going.
screen: `TWINS WHO FIGHT IN THE WOMB.` → `RED AND HAIRY; HOLDING THE HEEL.` → `A HUNTER AND A TENT-DWELLER.`

segments.voice: One day Jacob is cooking stew, and Esau comes in from the field, exhausted. In the JPS translation: "Let me swallow, I pray thee, some of this red, red pottage; for I am faint." He doesn't even name the food. Just: that red stuff. That's why, the Torah says, he was called Edom, red. And Jacob says: first sell me your birthright. The birthright, the bechorah, was the firstborn's place: in Deuteronomy, a double share of the inheritance, and in Rashi's reading, the family's sacred service too. Esau shrugs: "Behold, I am at the point to die; and what profit shall the birthright do to me?" He swears, and Jacob hands him bread and lentils. Now listen to the verbs, fast as a man eating: he ate, and drank, and rose up, and went his way. And then the Torah's own verdict: "So Esau despised his birthright." The rabbis add a detail that changes the scene. The Talmud says that on that very day, Abraham, their grandfather, had died. Lentils were a mourner's meal, the Talmud says: round, because mourning comes around to everyone. Jacob was cooking for a house in mourning, and Esau came in from the field without even noticing. And some readers are uneasy with Jacob here too. He made a deal with a starving brother. The Torah blames Esau for selling cheap; those readers also ask what kind of brother drives that bargain. Both things can be true. What's left on the table is the warning: something precious traded for one hot bowl, because it was right there, and you were hungry.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think about what you trade too cheaply when you're tired or hungry or bored. Sleep, traded for one more episode. A promise to your kid, traded for five more minutes on your phone. Your temper, traded for the pleasure of being right. Your quiet morning, traded for a scroll. Pick one. Notice the red stew in it: the thing that's right there and hot. Notice what you give up for it. If you pray, you can ask for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Bechorah, Hebrew for the birthright, what Esau traded for a bowl of stew. A birthright traded for lentils by a hungry twin, and the Torah's verdict: he despised it.
Your line: don't sell it for stew. Today, when you're about to trade something precious for something easy, pause for one breath first. Day fifty-three.

54.title: The stolen blessing (Genesis 27)
54.hook: goat skins, a blind father, and Esau's cry "Bless me, even me also, O my father"
54.howItsDone: Jews read this story in the Torah portion Toldot; on Friday nights many Jewish parents place their hands on their children's heads and bless each of them, one by one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bechorah, the birthright traded for lentils. Your line was don't sell it for stew. What did you almost trade too cheaply? Day fifty-four.

Isaac is old, and his eyes have gone dim. He calls in Esau, his favorite. Go hunt, he says, and make me the tasty food I love, so I can bless you before I die. Rebekah is listening. She calls Jacob, her favorite, and gives him a plan. Bring me two young goats; I'll cook them the way your father likes. You'll take the food in, and he'll bless you instead. Jacob hesitates. Esau is hairy and I'm smooth. If he touches me, I'll be caught, and I'll get a curse, not a blessing. And his mother answers, in the old JPS translation: "Upon me be thy curse, my son." So she dresses him in Esau's best clothes, and covers his hands and neck with goat skins. Today: Esau, the brother who came home too late.
screen: `A BLIND FATHER, A FAVORITE SON.` → `UPON ME BE THY CURSE.` → `GOAT SKINS ON HIS HANDS.`

segments.voice: Jacob goes in. Who are you, my son? I'm Esau, your firstborn. Isaac is uneasy. How did you find game so fast? Come close, let me feel you. He touches the goat-skin hands, and says one of the most famous lines in Genesis: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau." He blesses him anyway: the dew of heaven, the richness of the earth, may nations serve you. Jacob has barely left when Esau walks in with the meal. Who are you? I am your son, your firstborn, Esau. And the Torah says Isaac "trembled very exceedingly." Then Esau understands, and he cries out with a great and bitter cry: "Bless me, even me also, O my father." And again: "Hast thou but one blessing, my father?" And he lifts up his voice and weeps. This is one of the most painful moments in the Torah, and the rabbis didn't look away from it. A midrash says that Esau's cry was answered, many centuries later, in the book of Esther, when Mordecai, a descendant of Jacob, cries out in Persia with a great and bitter cry, the same words. The tears of the brother who was passed over were not forgotten. Readers argue about Rebekah: some say she acted on the prophecy that the elder would serve the younger; others see a family broken by favorites. Everyone here deceives or is deceived. But the voice that stays is Esau's, asking for what every child asks for: a blessing of my own.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone in your life who feels passed over. The sibling who wasn't the favorite. The coworker who didn't get the promotion. The kid who always gets picked last. The parent nobody calls. Picture their face. Hear their question: is there a blessing for me too? You can't undo what happened to them. But you can hold them for a minute with care. If you pray, you can bless them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Esau, the brother who came home too late and cried out, bless me, even me also, O my father.
Your line: bless me too. Today, find the person who feels passed over, and give them a blessing of their own: real praise, real time, real attention. Day fifty-four.

55.title: Jacob's ladder (Genesis 28:10–22)
55.hook: asleep on a stone, he dreams of angels going up and down
55.tomorrow: seven years like a few days
55.howItsDone: Jews read Jacob's dream in the Torah portion Vayetze; tradition credits Jacob with the evening prayer, Maariv, and HaMakom, the Place, is used as a name for God, as in the words said to comfort mourners.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Esau's cry, bless me, even me also. Your line was bless me too. Who got a blessing of their own from you? Day fifty-five.

Esau is furious. He says he'll kill his brother once their father dies. So Rebekah sends Jacob away, to her brother Laban in Haran. And Jacob, the quiet one who stayed in the tents, is suddenly alone on the road with nothing. No family, no flocks, no plan. The sun goes down. In the old JPS translation: "And he lighted upon the place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set." Not a town. Not an inn. Just the place, wherever he happened to be when it got dark. He takes some stones, puts them under his head, and lies down on the ground. Anyone who has spent a night in an airport, a hospital waiting room or a strange bed knows that place. Nowhere. And there, he dreams.
screen: `RUNNING FROM ESAU.` → `HE LIGHTED UPON THE PLACE.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: "And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven; and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it." Notice the order: ascending, then descending. You'd expect angels to come down from heaven first. Rashi, the medieval commentator, has an answer. The angels who had guarded Jacob in the land of Israel were going up, their shift over, and new angels, for the road ahead, were coming down. A changing of the guard over a sleeping man. Then God stands beside him and promises: the land, children like the dust of the earth, and "I am with thee, and will keep thee whithersoever thou goest." Jacob wakes up and says the sentence that gives today its line: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." He was sure he was nowhere. He was at the gate of heaven. He names the spot Beth-el, the house of God. Here's a small word with a big afterlife: the place. In later Hebrew, HaMakom, the Place, becomes one of the names for God. A midrash explains: God is the place of the world, and the world is not God's place. And the same Talmud passage we met with Isaac says that Jacob, lighting on the place at nightfall, began the evening prayer. In that view, the set is complete: Abraham the morning, Isaac the afternoon, Jacob the night. Jacob lay down in the dark, on a stone, in the middle of nowhere, and woke up saying that God had been in that nowhere all along.

If not, just give this ordinary place your full attention, the way you would a place that mattered. You don't have to feel anything special. The bell holds the time.
Jacob's ladder. A dream on a stone in the middle of nowhere: angels going up and down, and God standing beside him.
Your line: God was here all along. Today, stop in one ordinary place, a kitchen, a bus stop, a hallway, and call it holy. Day fifty-five.

56.title: Seven years like a few days (Genesis 29:1–20)
56.hook: Jacob works seven years for Rachel and they seem to him but a few days
56.howItsDone: Jews read Jacob's meeting with Rachel in the Torah portion Vayetze, and the verse about seven years seeming a few days is sometimes quoted in wedding speeches.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jacob's ladder, a stone for a pillow, and the gate of heaven. Your line was God was here all along. Which ordinary place did you call holy? Day fifty-six.

Jacob walks on, to the land of the east, and comes to a well in a field. Genesis loves a well: Hagar's, Rebekah's, Isaac's. There are shepherds lying around with their flocks, and a huge stone over the mouth of the well. They only roll it off when every shepherd has arrived, all together. And then Rachel comes, Laban's daughter, with her father's sheep. She's a shepherd. And Jacob, the quiet tent-dweller, walks up and rolls the great stone off the well by himself, and waters her whole flock. Then he kisses her, and lifts up his voice, and weeps. After the running, the stone pillow, the long road, he has found his mother's family. And he has found her.
screen: `ANOTHER WELL.` → `HE ROLLS THE STONE ALONE.` → `HE KISSES RACHEL, AND WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Laban, Rachel's father, takes Jacob in. After a month of Jacob working for nothing, Laban says: you shouldn't serve me for free. Name your wages. Now the Torah introduces the two daughters. Leah, the elder, whose eyes, it says, were tender, or weak: the Hebrew word can mean either, and readers disagree. And Rachel, beautiful in form and face. Jacob loves Rachel. So he names his price: I'll serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter. Seven years. No silver, no bride-price, just work. Then comes the verse, in the old JPS translation: "And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her." Stop there, because it's strange. When you love someone and you're waiting for them, don't days feel longer, not shorter? Anyone who has waited for a wedding, a baby, a soldier's return knows that. Commentators have wrestled with this. One answer: the love wasn't impatience. Jacob wasn't counting down, wishing the years away. He loved her so much that seven years of work seemed a small price, a few days' worth. The work itself became part of the love. Another reading hears it in hindsight: looking back, the years folded up like days. Either way, the verse makes a simple point: time is measured by the heart as well as the clock. And Jacob, who took a blessing by a trick, now earns a bride by years of honest work. Hold on to that. Tomorrow, the story turns.
screen: `NAME YOUR WAGES.` · `SEVEN YEARS FOR RACHEL.` · `SHOULDN'T LOVE MAKE IT LONGER?` · `THE WORK BECAME THE LOVE.` · then, large: `BUT A FEW DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one task in front of you today that you'll probably do while checking the clock. Cooking dinner. A long drive to pick someone up. Helping with homework. Caring for a parent. Now think of the person it's for. Picture their face. Let the task become something you give them, not something you get through. Notice if the time feels different. If you pray, you can offer the task as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Rachel, Laban's daughter, for whom Jacob served seven years that felt, the Torah says, like a few days, because of the love he had for her.
Your line: love shortens the time. Today, do one task for love, not the clock, and don't check how long it took. Day fifty-six.

original.note: Hebrew: like a few days. how seven years felt to Jacob.

trapdoor: what you thought: time flies when you're in love.
what it means: Jacob's love made seven years of work feel small, a price worth paying, not a countdown.
what a scholar hears: the puzzle commentators raise: longing should make time longer, so the verse is read as love without impatience, or as hindsight.
